items.statement: Assume countable choice. Let $D$ be a connected alternating regular link diagram with at least one crossing, and assume that every simple closed curve on its projection sphere transverse to $D$ in exactly two noncrossing points has a complementary disk containing no crossings. Then, for the represented smooth link $L$, every smooth sphere transverse to $L$ in exactly two points has a ball side containing no closed link component and a single boundary-parallel proper link arc. Here boundary-parallel means that the arc and an arc on the sphere cobound an embedded disk, with its natural endpoint corners, whose interior lies in that ball. Thus no two-point sphere decomposes $L$ into two nontrivial one-string ball tangles. Component orientations and any supplied labels are retained.

citations.quote: If a regular link diagram on $S^2$ is connected and alternating, then the represented link is nonsplit.

Assume countable choice. Let $D$ be a finite connected regular diagram representing a nonsplit smooth link $L$, with at least one crossing. Suppose $L$ admits a transverse two-point sphere with both side tangles nontrivial. Then the following model can be supplied.

Take its usual reference cornered crossing-ball picture $K$: the overpasses and underpasses are exact semicircles in unit crossing coordinates, and the remaining arcs lie on the projection sphere $P$. Its upper and lower open-side pieces $B_+,B_-$ are balls with product edge corners; their faces and the crossing balls cover $S^3$. There are disjoint closed smooth adapter balls $A_e$ about the finitely many corners of $K$, and a smooth link $L'$ ambient isotopic to $L$, equal to $K$ outside their interiors and equal to its semicircle arcs throughout the crossing balls. Inside the adapters the exterior arcs of $L'$ may leave $P$.

There is a smooth sphere $T$ with two transverse punctures on $L'$ outside the crossing and adapter balls and with both side tangles nontrivial, disjoint from every $A_e$, such that its crossing-ball pieces are finite ordered quadrilateral saddle disks. The reference open-side pieces $T\cap B_\pm$ are disks; their intersection circles with the reference shifted spheres have nonempty bubble words and meet each hemisphere at most once. These words use $K$ on the reference common face, where it agrees with $L'$ at every puncture. All incidence statements are taken in the reference face-and-corner model; individual geometric disk applications use inward smooth roundings of the open-side balls. Their intersections with $T$ have exactly the same piece topology and circle incidences.

Assume countable choice. Let $D$ be a connected alternating regular link diagram with at least one crossing, and let a closed embedded surface be transverse to the represented link and both shifted spheres. Suppose its crossing-ball pieces are finite ordered levels of the explicit quadrilateral saddle model and it is in bubble standard position. Then no cyclic bubble word has the form $P^iS^j$ with $i\ge0$ and $j>0$. Moreover every bubble word has at least two $P$'s. The assertion applies to both shifted spheres and does not require reducedness of the diagram.

Let a sphere $T$ be decomposed by finitely many crossing balls and two complementary open-side balls, with compatible corner conventions. Suppose each crossing-ball piece is a quadrilateral saddle disk, with two upper and two lower hemisphere arcs and four distinct equatorial corners, and each open-side piece is a disk. Let $s$ be the number of saddle disks, and let $u,\ell$ be the numbers of upper and lower disk pieces. Along the common projection face the upper and lower pieces are glued, and at each equatorial corner one upper piece, one lower piece and its saddle meet in the usual three-sector chart. Then
$$u+\ell-s=2.$$
In particular if there is exactly one upper and one lower piece, there are no saddles. Link punctures on the common-face arcs do not change this count.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

derivations.claim: By [F1] the link is nonsplit. Suppose there were a two-point sphere whose two side tangles were nontrivial, allowing closed components. Apply [F2] to obtain the smooth link $L'$ and normalized sphere $T$, with its reference projection sphere $P$, crossing balls and adapter balls. Both actual link punctures lie on the common projection face, outside the crossing and adapter balls, so every puncture is counted once in the upper words and once in the lower words. Each total puncture count is therefore two.

Every upper word has at least two punctures by [F3], and at least one upper circle exists because there are two punctures. Thus there is exactly one upper circle. The same reasoning gives exactly one lower circle. Since all open-side pieces are disks by [F2], each has one boundary circle, and every cut circle is incident to precisely one such disk. Hence $u=\ell=1$. The reference corner charts give the three-sector disk gluing required in [F4], so its equation yields $s=0$.

The sphere now misses every crossing ball and adapter ball. On their complement the two shifted spheres agree with $P$, so their single intersection circle is the same smooth circle $C=T\cap P$. It is transverse to the represented diagram in exactly the two punctures, both noncrossing points, and avoids every crossing disk. The hypothesis on $D$ supplies a closed complementary disk $\Delta\subset P$ containing no crossing. Its diagram portion is exactly one embedded proper arc. Indeed there are exactly two boundary endpoints, no vertex inside and no intersection among strands there. Any additional circle would be an entire component of the projection disjoint from the rest, contrary to connectedness of $D$ and the presence of the two-point arc.

The interior of $\Delta$ lies in one ball side $U$ of $T$, by [F5]. The other disk of $P\setminus C$ lies on the opposite side: transversality along $C$ puts the two local projection sides in opposite components of $S^3\setminus T$, and connectedness keeps each disk on that side. Every crossing ball is disjoint from $T$ and contains its projected crossing in the other projection disk, since $\Delta$ has no crossings and $C$ misses the whole crossing balls. Each connected crossing ball therefore lies on the opposite ball side from $U$. Its endpoint adapters do too: each is connected, disjoint from $T$, and meets its crossing ball. Thus all departures of $L'$ from the common projection face lie outside $U$.

Consequently $L'\cap U$ is precisely the one proper arc in $\Delta$ from step 3.1, with no closed components. That arc cuts $\Delta$ into disks by [F5]. Choose either one. Its boundary is the link arc together with an arc of $C\subset T$, and its interior lies in $\operatorname{int}U$, since $T\cap P=C$. The disk is smooth on its faces and has the compatible quarter-disk corners at its two endpoints required of a boundary-parallelism disk. Thus this side tangle is trivial, contradicting the two nontrivial sides of $T$ in [F2]. No such nontrivial two-point decomposition exists.

For any sphere meeting a closed link twice, its two crossings belong to one component and divide that component into one proper arc on either side; every other component stays on a single side. This follows by successive changes of ball side, using [F5]. If neither one-string side tangle were trivial, both would be nontrivial, which step 5.1 ruled out. Hence every such sphere has the stated trivial side. Ambient isotopy from $L$ to $L'$ transports spheres, ball sides and bridge disks, so the conclusion applies to the original smooth link. All these isotopies transport component orientations and labels.

boundaries.reason: The Statement assumes a connected diagram with a crossing and an actual two-point sphere.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 proves zero saddles; steps 3.1–5.1 construct the trivial side.
Steps 2.1–3.1 identify one upper disk, one lower disk and one proper arc.

boundaries.reason: Regular crossings, transverse two-point spheres and noncrossing punctures are assumed.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 3.1 and 5.1 retain both transverse endpoints and the natural bridge-disk corners.
Steps 1.1 and 4.1 explicitly inherit countable choice from the actual-model normalization and sphere suppliers.

axioms.use: Countable choice is inherited from the smooth-model normalization, the surface Jordan-disk supplier and smooth Schoenflies. The word and Euler counts are finite.
